claims.text: The hypothesis concerns face-centered-cubic Fe-Co-Ni-based high- or medium-entropy alloys, including CoCrFeMnNi and CoNiCr.
The targeted property is the orbital-moment contribution to magnetic anisotropy energy.
Static or floating-spin calculations give zero or negligible moments for Co, Cr, and Ni in paramagnetic fcc CoCrFeMnNi.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations induce sizable magnetic moments on Co, Cr, and Ni in fcc and hcp CoCrFeMnNi.
Magnetically driven chemical short-range order forms unbalanced magnetic sublattices and produces ferrimagnetism in these alloys.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations alter magnetic entropy and internal-energy contributions to free energy.
Magneto-volume coupling and longitudinal spin fluctuations suppress the orbital-moment contribution to magnetic anisotropy.
Chemical short-range order and magnetic frustration cause strange metallicity.
Chemical short-range order and magnetic frustration reduce coercivity.
CoNiCr exhibits an extremely small magnetic moment at 5 K.
CoNiCr exhibits resistivity that is linear in temperature and is identified as strange metallicity.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations affect the temperature-dependent stacking-fault energy and phase stability of CoCrFeMnNi.
Conventional floating-spin calculations fail to reproduce temperature-dependent stacking-fault energy and phase stability accurately.
The relevant modeling range is 50–1200 K, with varying Wigner-Seitz radius and comparison of fcc and hcp structures.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations and short-range order explain a discrepancy between static DFT predictions and cryogenic experimental magnetic behavior.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to ordered B2 phases or strongly ferromagnetic systems where orbital moments are more pronounced.
Omitting explicit phonons may contribute to discrepancies between predicted and experimental critical temperatures.
Ferromagnetic matrix phases and complex asperomagnetic states can make direct experimental isolation of orbital-moment effects difficult.
Temperature variation and annealing can be used to control longitudinal spin fluctuations and chemical short-range order for an XMCD and torque-magnetometry test.

The hypothesis is falsified if the orbital moment remains significant and strongly correlated with magnetic anisotropy despite longitudinal spin fluctuations and short-range order, or if magnetic anisotropy energy does not decrease as temperature increases.
